question: What is the penalty for drink driving in Singapore for a first conviction?
answer:
The penalty for drink driving in Singapore for a first conviction is a fine of not less than $2,000 and not more than $10,000 or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 12 months or to both. [Road Traffic Act 1961 — s 67(1)] 

Additionally, the court convicting the person is to order that the person be disqualified from holding or obtaining a driving licence for a period of 2 years starting on the date of the person’s conviction. [Road Traffic Act 1961 — s 67(2)(a)]

question: What is the default speed limit on roads in Singapore?
answer:
According to Source 1 [Road Traffic (Restriction of Speed on Roads) Notification — para 2], the default speed limit on roads in Singapore, except for specific zones or areas mentioned in sub-paragraphs (2), (3), and (3A), is:

"...the speed of all motor vehicles travelling along any road or part of a road shall not exceed — (a) in the case of the roads or parts thereof set out in the First to Sixth Schedules, the speed specified in those Schedules; and (b) in any other case, 50 kilometres per hour."

Therefore, the default speed limit on roads in Singapore is 50 kilometres per hour.

question: Is it compulsory to have third-party motor insurance in Singapore?
answer:
According to Source 1 [Motor Vehicles (Third-Party Risks and Compensation) Act 1960 — s 3], it is compulsory to have third-party motor insurance in Singapore.

(1) Subject to the provisions of this Act, it is not lawful for any person to use or to cause or permit any other person to use — (a) a motor vehicle in Singapore; or (b) a motor vehicle which is registered in Singapore in any territory specified in the Schedule, unless there is in force in relation to the use of the motor vehicle by that person or that other person (as the case may be) a policy of insurance or a security in respect of third-party risks that complies with the requirements of this Act.

Therefore, yes, it is compulsory to have third-party motor insurance in Singapore.

ground_truth: Yes. A person must not use or permit another to use a motor vehicle unless there is in force a policy of insurance covering third-party risks. It is an offence to use an uninsured motor vehicle.
